overview: This file documents the Japanese administration’s phased removal of small Chinese silver coins (hsiaoyang-chien) from circulation in the Kwantung Leased Territory and their replacement with Bank of Chosen notes and legally recognized coins. It contains an American consular report announcing the policy, State Department memoranda explaining its connection to currency and foreign-exchange control, a subsequent despatch transmitting the implementing legislation, and translations of three Japanese ordinances prohibiting circulation after April 1, 1936, arranging government purchases of the withdrawn coins, and immediately banning further imports. Together, the documents show how a colonial monetary policy moved from press announcement to detailed legal and administrative enforcement.

subfiles.title: Despatch announcing prohibition of small Chinese silver coinage
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the announced plan to prohibit small Chinese silver coins in the Kwantung Leased Territory beginning in April 1936.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports a December 14 newspaper account of an announcement by the chief of the Kwantung Bureau. Because officials recognized the difficulty of abruptly withdrawing the coins, the prohibition would be introduced gradually while Bank of Chosen “gold” notes replaced them in contracts and payments. The bureau also expected to arrange the purchase of existing coins from their holders at a reasonable price.

subfiles.title: State Department memorandum on ordinances for taking up silver coinage
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Explains that an attached Dairen despatch transmits ordinances implementing the withdrawal of silver coinage from the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies a Dairen despatch of December 23, 1935, as transmitting translations of the implementing ordinances. It characterizes the affected currency as mostly Chinese silver coinage and connects the material with the earlier Dairen despatches of December 10 and 16.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting ordinances prohibiting small silver coinage
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits three ordinances governing the prohibition, redemption, and importation of small silver coins in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The consul forwards Imperial Ordinance No. 313 and Kwantung Bureau Ordinances Nos. 73 and 74. The measures prohibit circulation after April 1, 1936, provide for designated agencies to purchase the coins between April 1 and June 30, and immediately prohibit additional imports. Although the cover-page OCR gives an inconsistent date, the State Department memorandum and all three enclosure headings identify the despatch as dated December 23, 1935.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 313 on hsiaoyang-chien
subfiles.about: Prohibits hsiaoyang-chien after April 1, 1936, and establishes their purchase and replacement by Bank of Chosen currency.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance prohibits circulation of hsiaoyang-chien in the Kwantung territory after April 1, 1936, while requiring the government to purchase the coins from holders at designated places. Obligations created by March 31 may still be settled with the silver coins or Bank of Chosen currency, but later obligations must use Bank of Chosen notes or lawful coins. Further implementation details are delegated to the Japanese ambassador.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 73 on purchasing hsiaoyang-chien
subfiles.from: Jiro Minami, Ambassador Extraordinary of Japan
subfiles.about: Sets the institutions and period for government-authorized purchases of withdrawn hsiaoyang-chien.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance provides that designated banks and exchange companies will purchase the small silver coins under Imperial Ordinance No. 313. Commissions, quantities, values, and market prices were to be announced separately. The authorized purchase period would run from April 1 through June 30, 1936.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 74 prohibiting imports of hsiaoyang-chien
subfiles.about: Immediately prohibits importing or preparing to import small silver coins into the Kwantung territory and prescribes criminal penalties.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance bans both the importation of small silver coins and preparations to import them. Violators face up to one year of imprisonment at hard labor, a fine below 200 yen, or both. It also extends liability to legal persons, principals, and employers represented by offending agents or employees.

subfiles.title: State Department memorandum on currency control in Kwantung
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the currency-control purpose of the December 10 and 16 Dairen despatches.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that the Kwantung government intended to take up the territory’s circulating silver coinage, most of which was Chinese. It describes the policy as an effort to secure closer control of both currency and foreign exchange. Paper money would be introduced gradually.

interest: The file provides a compact documentary sequence from public announcement through formal implementation of a colonial currency reform. Particularly useful are the translated ordinances, which reveal the transition timetable, the treatment of existing obligations, the reliance on banks and exchange companies, and the criminal penalties used to prevent replenishment of the withdrawn currency. The accompanying consular and State Department memoranda place these technical measures in the broader context of Japanese efforts to control foreign exchange and monetary circulation in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
